Context: In `1996` and `1997`, World Chess Champion Garry Kasparov played `text(two)` chess matches against a supercomputer named Deep Blue, created by the company IBM. The matches placed Kasparov’s intelligence against the computer’s artificial intelligence.
Title: Passage 2: from How Life Imitates Chess
Author: by Garry Kasparov
Content: After my `text(first)` match with Deep Blue in `1996` in Philadelphia received so much publicity, IBM threw its full weight behind a `text(six-game)` rematch in `text(May 1997)` to be held in downtown Manhattan. In `1996`, I lost the `text(first)` game of the match, but after that wake-up call I came back to win `text(three)` games and easily defeat the computer `4-2`. For the rematch IBM claimed “Deeper Blue” was `text(twice)` as fast and much smarter. They had hired human Grandmasters to work full-time “teaching” the computer by improving its evaluation function.

The media attention for the `text(first)` game of the rematch was beyond that of a world championship. Over `text(three hundred)` journalists were accredited, and the `text(five-hundred-seat)` auditorium sold out at `text($25 per ticket)`. Of course I was nervous. Being human, I was unable to ignore all of these distractions, unlike my silicon¹ opponent. But I played well enough to win the `text(first)` game with white². The `text(second)` game would, however, change the course of the match, and of human-machine competition.

I’ve talked about computers and their inability to make long-term plans. They calculate variations in a linear way, examining `text(each move)` in turn, searching deeper and deeper. Even at Deep Blue’s `text(200 million)` moves `text(per second)`, it took it a long time to see far enough ahead to play competent strategic chess. It would occasionally make silly moves no strong human would consider, and it did this in its loss in game `text(one)`. Game `text(two)` was an entirely different matter. . . . Instead of going for a short-term advantage, it closed in for the kill. Faced with a losing position and stunned by the godlike quality of the machine’s play, I resigned.

I soon received an even greater shock. It turned out that the final position of the `text(second)` game was not a losing `text(one)` for me after all. With its last move the computer had blundered, and I had resigned in a drawn position! It felt like being kicked in the stomach after already being knocked down. When I was shown the drawing line, I realized that I would have continued on against any human. . . .

I missed a clear win in the `text(fourth)` game, and by then I was exhausted and confused. Was something fishy going on, or was Deep Blue really so strong? In the `text(fifth)` game I again missed good winning chances, so the match remained tied with `text(one)` win apiece and `text(three)` draws. Everything was set for a showdown in game `text(six)`, but looking back today, I see my fate had already been sealed.

It took only `text(nineteen)` moves for me to resign the worst game of my career and lose the match. I was simply in no condition to play chess by that point, and I made an infantile blunder in the opening. After a few more feeble moves the game and the match were over. I was ashamed of my performance and for letting the mysterious `text(second)` game get to me.
